Chapter 5: Planning for Success — Strategic and Possibility-Oriented Thinking
Now that you’ve built a foundation of intentional, creative, focused, and reflective thought, it’s time to look ahead.
This is where planning and purposeful action come into play. And to really make progress, you’ll need to develop two essential habits: thinking strategically, and staying open to new possibilities.
Let’s start with strategic thinking. Imagine it as the art of mapping out your journey—from where you are, to where you want to be. It’s about setting clear goals, spotting any obstacles ahead, and figuring out the best steps to get you to your destination. Strategic thinkers are a lot like chess players—they’re always planning several moves in advance, weighing the potential outcome of each decision.
Here’s what makes strategic thinking really effective:
You define specific, measurable objectives.
You break down big goals into smaller, actionable steps.
You identify possible challenges and have backup plans ready.
And you allocate your resources—like time, energy, or money—where they’ll make the most difference.
This mindset is especially important if you’re in a leadership role or running a business—where the environment is always changing and resources are often limited.
Picture an entrepreneur launching a new business. It’s not enough to just have a vision. They need a detailed plan for developing their product, marketing it, and growing their company. By thinking strategically, they can actually turn those ideas into reality.
But strategy alone isn’t enough. That’s where possibility-oriented thinking comes in. This is about keeping your mind open to new opportunities and different paths. Instead of asking, “Will this work?” you start wondering, “What else could work? Is there a better way?”
This mindset keeps you from getting stuck. It sparks innovation, especially when things don’t go as planned.
Think of it like being a navigator crossing the ocean. You know where you want to end up, but as the winds and currents shift, you might have to adjust your course. Possibility-oriented thinkers stay flexible, and aren’t afraid to change their approach when new information or unexpected challenges pop up.
So, how do you develop this habit? Here are a few things that successful, possibility-oriented people do:
They stay curious and open-minded, even when plans seem locked in.
They invite input and fresh ideas from others.
They see setbacks as a chance to explore new directions.
And they’re always scanning the horizon for new trends or changes in the environment.
Just think about a nonprofit organization that suddenly faces funding cuts. Instead of just cutting back on services, the team looks for new ways to generate revenue. They might try partnering with other groups, or even launch new programs to adapt. By blending strategic planning with an open mind, the organization doesn’t just survive—it finds creative ways to keep moving forward.
When you put strategic thinking and possibility-oriented thinking together, you get the best of both worlds. Strategy gives you structure and direction. Openness to possibility keeps you adaptable and resilient.
So, you can chase big goals—but you’re also ready to pivot and grow as life throws new challenges your way.
